findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The Council reports no liquidity risks in its 12-month cash flow forecast and no cash flow issues affecting creditor payments in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council maintains a rolling 12-month cash flow forecast to support financial planning. It says the Council met creditor payments as they fell due throughout the year.
findings.matters: A cash position with no liquidity risks forecast is a point lenders and treasury teams will weigh alongside reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: Rolling 12-month cash flow forecast
findings.quote: Current forecasts indicate no liquidity risks

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Arcadis's asset management review proposed a phased disposal programme for elements of the investment estate to generate capital receipts, reported to Cabinet in April 2026.
findings.detail: The recommendations included adopting a Strategic Asset Management Plan and developing a Core Asset Portfolio prioritising heritage, leisure and community assets. Each disposal is subject to business case and options appraisal before Cabinet approval.
findings.matters: A council planning disposals from an investment estate to fund reinvestment is a capital-funding decision that lenders and peer councils will watch.
findings.quote: Consideration of a phased disposal programme for elements of the investment estate to generate capital receipts

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The Local Government Reorganisation decision that would abolish Tamworth Borough Council from 1 April 2028 was paused on 7 September 2026 pending a full review.
findings.detail: The paper says the 16 July 2026 decision confirmed the successor as South and Mid Staffordshire Council. The Council will continue service delivery as planned until at least April 2028 while the review is under way.
findings.matters: A reorganisation that could end the council's existence in 2028 affects how lenders and finance directors across the sector assess its long-term funding and debt position.
findings.figures: Abolition date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: However, on 7 September 2026 the Secretary of State announced a full review of the LGR programme and as such paused the activity.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The Council recruited to a key finance role previously filled by temporary staff in 2025/26, and the LGA workforce action plan recommendation is recorded as resolved.
findings.detail: The paper says the substantive appointment to the Assistant Director Finance role has strengthened senior experience in the team. It also says the Finance team has been recruited to full establishment.
findings.matters: Moving a finance-critical role from temporary to substantive staff, and closing a prior-year recommendation, is the kind of change a finance director elsewhere would compare against their own team.
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council was able to recruit to a key role which had been filled previously by temporary staff.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The Procurement Strategy review due in January 2026 did not take place as planned and had not been carried out by the end of 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says officers have confirmed the review will be reported to the Corporate Management Team in 2026/27 as part of quarterly updates. The auditor found no evidence of unfair procurement.
findings.matters: A missed review date for a strategy written to meet the Procurement Act 2023 is a deadline other councils may face in the same transition.
findings.figures: Review due January 2026
findings.quote: This review did not take place as planned and therefore had not been updated by the end of the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The 2025/26 accounts audit is ongoing, with no significant issues identified to date and the audit certificate not yet issued.
findings.detail: The paper says the auditor is awaiting group auditor instructions from the NAO before it can conclude the audit, and that Whole of Government Accounts confirmation is still needed. No matters are reported from component auditor work so far.
findings.matters: A year-end audit still open at the November committee, pending NAO instructions, is a timing point other finance teams in the same audit cycle will be tracking.
findings.quote: Our testing and review of the financial statements to date has not identified any significant issues

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Value for money rating for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness moved from Green in 2024/25 to Amber in 2025/26, with two recommendations.
findings.detail: The auditor says there are no significant weaknesses in these arrangements but has made two recommendations for improvement. The Governance criterion is also Amber, with one recommendation.
findings.matters: A rating moving from Green to Amber on the same criterion is a visible change in auditor view that peer councils and lenders can read directly from the VFM table.
findings.figures: Amber (2025/26), Green (2024/25); two recommendations; Governance Amber with one recommendation
findings.quote: We have identified two recommendations for further improving arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Internal Audit gave a reasonable assurance opinion for 2025/26 and found no significant weaknesses, with limited assurance on Cyber Incident Response Plan and Planned Maintenance.
findings.detail: The paper says the number of outstanding audit recommendations has fallen significantly over recent years, particularly high-priority ones. It also says management actions are in progress on the two limited-assurance areas.
findings.matters: A reasonable assurance opinion, with the two limited-assurance areas named, is the baseline other councils' internal audit committees will compare against.
findings.figures: Two areas with limited assurance
findings.quote: Within the report, the Head of Internal Audit provided a reasonable assurance opinion

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Ankerside Shopping Centre service charge expenditure was £1.681m against a £1.184m budget, £497k above budget, and contributions to Lichfield District Council were £582k above budget.
findings.detail: The paper identifies these two items among the most significant adverse directorate variances in Environment, Culture and Wellbeing and Corporate Asset Management and Heritage. It does not give a cause for the Ankerside overspend beyond the variance itself.
findings.matters: Service charge overspends on commercial property and shared-service payments to a partner council are the cost pressures a finance director needs to track on an investment estate.
findings.figures: £1.681m Ankerside service charge expenditure; £1.184m budget; £497k above budget; £582k Lichfield District Council contributions above budget
findings.quote: service charge expenditure for Ankerside Shopping Centre of £1.681m - £497k above the budget of £1.184m.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Auditors have raised an amber recommendation that capital re-profiling reports should show potential overruns and impacts on service delivery.
findings.detail: The paper says budget holder comments in monthly and quarterly reporting do not show potential cost overruns when projects move between years. The management response agrees that comments on re-profiled projects should cover additional costs and grant conditions.
findings.matters: A specific auditor recommendation on capital re-profiling reporting is the kind of finding other councils will check their own reporting against.
findings.figures: Amber recommendation (2025/26)
findings.quote: the Council should consider how this can be added to enhance the capital reporting for major projects

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Capital slippage took £17,426k of General Fund and £8,762k of HRA re-profiling from 2024/25 into 2025/26, with a further £11,269k and £12,839k carried into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says officers understand the reasons for the slippage but members receive limited reporting of them. Auditors have raised a recommendation that potential overruns from carried-over projects be reported, particularly where grant funding sets timing conditions.
findings.matters: Repeated slippage across two years raises the cost and deliverability risk on schemes, which finance officers at other councils will be checking in their own capital programmes.
findings.figures: General Fund capital budget £21,219k incl. £17,426k re-profiled from 2024/25; £11,269k re-profiled into 2026/27; HRA capital budget £20,040k incl. £8,762k re-profiled; £12,839k re-profiled into 2026/27
findings.quote: There is a further re-profiling into 2026/27 totalling £11,269k.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The Housing Revenue Account outturn showed an adverse variance of £1,029k against budget, with HRA balances reduced to £2,818k.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the HRA variance largely to housing management and repairs expenditure pressures. It says the closing balance was marginally below the level anticipated when the budget was approved.
findings.matters: An HRA overspend that cuts balances is a recurring pressure for stock-holding councils, and this figure gives a direct comparison point.
findings.figures: £1,029k adverse HRA variance; £2,818k HRA balances
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) revenue outturn reporting showed an adverse variance of £1,029k compared to budget

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: General Fund usable reserves stood at £27,583k at 31 March 2026, including £18,760k of earmarked reserves, and the Council plans to keep using reserves to fund in-year deficits.
findings.detail: The paper says the current strategy of using usable reserves to fund in-year deficits is one the Council recognises is not sustainable in the longer term. The Chief Finance Officer's February 2026 statement put expected General Fund reserves at 31 March 2026 at £17.81m and said they would balance budgets until 2028/29.
findings.matters: Reserves funding in-year deficits with a stated end point is the central question for any council's medium-term solvency.
findings.figures: £27,583k General Fund usable reserves; £18,760k earmarked reserves; £17.81m expected General Fund reserves (S25 statement); £11.2m expected HRA reserves; sufficient until 2028/29
findings.quote: which it recognises is not sustainable in the longer term

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy shows a forecast deficit in each year to 2030/31, with a cumulative deficit of £13,163k.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 General Fund budget forecasts a £1,096k deficit despite a 2.99% council tax increase, due to pay awards estimated at 3% and inflationary uplifts at 2.8%. The paper says the position requires savings of £3.5m a year from 2030/31 if usable reserves are fully used before then.
findings.matters: A stated annual savings requirement from 2030/31 gives lenders and peer councils a specific gap to measure the Financial Resilience Plan against.
findings.figures: £13,163k cumulative MTFS deficit; £1,096k 2026/27 deficit; 2.99% council tax increase; 3% pay award estimate; 2.8% inflationary uplifts; £3.5m annual savings from 2030/31
findings.quote: with a cumulative deficit over the life of the MTFS totalling £13,163k.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: The auditor reports that savings plans were delivered with success in 2025/26, and that Financial Sustainability is rated Green with no recommendations.
findings.detail: The paper describes 2025/26 as the first implementation year of the Financial Resilience Plan and says the reporting to members set out the implications of not delivering. It rates Financial Sustainability Green for both 2024/25 and 2025/26.
findings.matters: An auditor's explicit comment on savings delivery is a rare external check on whether a council's savings plan is landing.
findings.figures: Financial Sustainability rated Green in 2025/26 and 2024/25
findings.quote: Work has been undertaken with success in 2025/26 to deliver savings plans

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Zero-based budgeting produced a General Fund net savings plan of £2,016k for 2025/26, the first year of the Financial Resilience Plan.
findings.detail: The paper says the zero-based budgeting exercise was a key output of the plan and that savings were tracked by service area in quarterly monitoring. It also says the HRA budget showed net cost increases of £1,624k over the same period.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare a council's zero-based savings target and its tracked delivery against their own plans.
findings.figures: £2,016k net savings plan (General Fund); £1,624k HRA net cost increases
findings.quote: The result of the changes made to budgets following this exercise was a net savings plan of £2,016k for the General Fund in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Draft Auditor's Annual Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Tamworth's 2025/26 General Fund outturn moved to a £258k deficit from a budgeted £150k surplus, a £408k negative variance funded through general fund reserves.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the July 2026 Cabinet outturn showed the deficit against a budgeted surplus. The largest adverse directorate variances were Environment, Culture and Wellbeing (£565k) and Corporate Asset Management and Heritage (£286k).
findings.matters: It shows a council closing a year with a drawdown on reserves to cover an adverse variance, which is the position other councils with similar pressures will be tracking.
findings.figures: £258k deficit; £150k surplus budgeted; £408k negative variance; £565k; £286k
findings.quote: reflecting a £408k negative variance against budget which was funded through general fund reserves.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Four prior-year audit recommendations recorded as resolved, including the council dwelling reconciliation and cash flow balancing figure
findings.detail: The four items under the 'Prior Year Issues – Resolved' heading are the council dwelling register reconciliation, the cash flow balancing figure, operating lease supporting documentation, and senior management journal postings. The auditor reports that the Council housing stock spreadsheet was updated, that cash flow no longer needs a balancing figure, and that no evidence issues arose on operating lease receivables.
findings.matters: Closing prior-year recommendations shows whether a council's remediation has worked, which other councils can use when setting their own audit action plans.
findings.figures: Cash flow balancing difference of £188k in 2024/25 (no balancing figure needed in 2025/26). Council dwellings variance of £512k in 2024/25.
findings.quote: Processes were implemented so that no balancing figure was required in 2025/26, therefore this recommendation is resolved.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Statement of Accounts for 2025/26 published on the Council's website ahead of the statutory deadline
findings.detail: The auditor received the unaudited financial statements in line with the agreed timetable, and the Statement of Accounts was published before the statutory deadline. Information requested during fieldwork was generally provided promptly, though there were delays in some areas, mainly from the external valuer and the pension fund auditor.
findings.matters: Meeting the publication deadline is a measurable result that finance directors at other councils, many of which have missed recent deadlines, can compare against.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: The Statement of Accounts was also published on the Council’s website in advance of the statutory deadline.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Auditor has identified no significant weaknesses in the Council's value for money arrangements for 2025/26
findings.detail: The auditor assessed financial sustainability, governance, and economy, efficiency and effectiveness, based on a management self-assessment and follow-up work. The full value for money findings are in the separate Auditor's Annual Report.
findings.matters: A clean value for money conclusion is the main external assurance on financial sustainability and governance that lenders and peer finance directors look for.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: We have not identified any significant weaknesses and the results of the Value for money work are reported separately in our Auditor’s Annual Report.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Additional value for money work on asset disposal arrangements, prompted by an elected member's questions, adds to the audit fee
findings.detail: The auditor says it spent senior time following up questions from an elected member about the Council's asset disposal arrangements and whether they meet best value. This work is still ongoing. The total audit fee is £168,750 plus TBC, against a planning-stage fee of £165,750. A further fee variation for PPE disclosure work is also TBC.
findings.matters: A member-driven best value question adding to audit fees is a governance point that other councils facing similar questions about disposals would want to know about.
findings.figures: Final fee £168,750 plus TBC (planning-stage fee £165,750; PSAA scale fee £165,750; 2024/25 total £195,957). Pension surplus variation £3,000.
findings.quote: following up questions raised by an elected member of the Council on the Council’s asset disposal arrangements and whether they constitute best value.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Key finance team members were unavailable to the auditors on most days of the on-site audit fieldwork
findings.detail: Following last year's audit, the Executive Director of Finance agreed to an on-site presence during fieldwork. The auditor says it had a presence, but key finance staff were not accessible on most days because of working practices at the Council, which reduced the value of the time on site.
findings.matters: Finance teams at other councils that agree on-site audit presence may face the same gap between an agreed plan and staff availability.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: there was a lack of access to key members of the finance team during the majority of the days on site owing to working practices at the Council.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Capital accounting entries produced by a temporary member of staff, with no substantive post holder for capital accounting
findings.detail: The auditor rated this Amber and reports that capital queries took longer than expected to resolve. A temporary member of staff worked from March to June 2026 on the final accounts. The management response says an Assistant Director of Finance who started in March now leads on PPE and fixed assets, with a Project Accountant for capital monitoring.
findings.matters: Dependence on temporary staff for capital accounting is a staffing risk that finance directors at other councils with similar vacancies will recognise.
findings.figures: Rated Amber. Temporary staff March to June 2026.
findings.quote: It does not have a substantive member of the finance team responsible for capital accounting.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Investment property valuation of £742k posted incorrectly to the fixed asset register, with the paper giving two different treatments
findings.detail: The auditor found that the investment property valuation was incorrectly posted to the fixed asset register. The adjusted items table records the £742k as corrected in the statements. The management letter describes it as an unadjusted difference of £742k, and management has agreed to introduce a formal reconciliation for future years.
findings.matters: Mispostings between valuation reports and asset registers are a control weakness that other councils with large property portfolios will check for in their own reconciliations.
findings.figures: £742k (CIES Cr; balance sheet Dr); £742k unadjusted difference per management letter.
findings.quote: On completing our audit procedures over the investment property valuation for 2025/26, we identified that the Council had incorrectly posted the asset valuations to the fixed asset register.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Auditor anticipates an unmodified opinion on the 2025/26 accounts, subject to outstanding items including PPE disclosures and NAO group instructions
findings.detail: The audit is described as largely complete. The auditor cannot yet issue the audit certificate because it is waiting for group audit instructions from the NAO for the Whole of Government Accounts return. Work on land and buildings disclosures is still open, and the auditor has not yet confirmed the revised Note 14 classifications received on 12 November.
findings.matters: A council's accounts cannot be closed until the certificate is issued, and an open PPE disclosure issue is a common source of delay for councils with large revaluation programmes.
findings.figures: Materiality £1,599,000 (2% of gross expenditure).
findings.quote: Subject to the satisfactory finalisation of these points, we anticipate issuing an unmodified audit report.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Auditor has not yet concluded the pension valuation risk, with assurances from the Staffordshire Pension Fund auditor still outstanding
findings.detail: The audit cannot yet fully conclude on the significant risk over the pension net liability. The auditor says it needs assurances from the Staffordshire Pension Fund auditor on membership, contributions, benefits and fund asset valuation data, including the triennial valuation.
findings.matters: Council pension liabilities depend on pool and fund auditor assurances, so delays in those assurances can hold up a council's own accounts.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: As at the date of this report, we have yet to receive necessary assurances from the auditor of Staffordshire Pension Fund.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Pension fund net surplus before asset ceiling moved from £31.2m to £37.2m in 2025/26, with none of the surplus recognised under IFRIC 14
findings.detail: The actuary's asset ceiling report concludes that, under IFRIC 14, none of the surplus should be recognised. IFRIC 14 also requires an additional liability for agreed past service contributions, which the paper puts at £3.8m at 31 March 2026. The discount rate moved from 5.8% to 6.2%.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with an LGPS surplus will face the same IFRIC 14 asset ceiling question and past service contribution liability.
findings.figures: £31.2m to £37.2m (surplus before asset ceiling); £3.8m past service contributions liability; discount rate 5.8% to 6.2%.
findings.quote: Before consideration of the impact of an asset ceiling, the pension valuation on the LGPS has moved from a net surplus position of £31.2m to a net surplus position of £37.2m.

findings.paper_title: Tamworth BC 2025-26 - Audit Completion Report (for November 2026 Committee)
findings.headline: Joint Waste Fleet lease liability difference of £747k left unadjusted, with the IFRS 16 recommendation from 2024/25 still unresolved
findings.detail: The auditor reports that the lease treatment used in the prior year has continued, leaving the Council's share of the right-of-use asset and lease liability understated. Lichfield District Council, as host authority, is not changing its accounting treatment, and the auditors did not agree on the approach in a March 2026 meeting. The management update states the impact will reduce over time as the lease liability reduces.
findings.matters: Any council in a joint service arrangement with a host authority may face the same disagreement over IFRS 16 treatment, and lenders see a recurring unadjusted misstatement on a shared arrangement.
findings.figures: Unadjusted: £21k CIES (Dr); £747k balance sheet (Cr); £768k balance sheet (Dr). 2024/25 understatement of £780k.
findings.quote: there remains an understatement of the Council’s share of the RoU assets and lease liabilities, as set out in section 7.

findings.headline: The Local Plan has completed Regulation 19 consultation, with submission preparation for December 2026

findings.matters: Completion of a statutory consultation stage is a milestone in the council's planning and housing delivery timetable, and the paper shows the next deadline.

findings.quote: The Local Plan has successfully completed Reg.19 consultation.

findings.headline: Market Street refurbishment has a high likelihood of delay to completion due to the condition of the building being "poorer than thought
findings.detail: The Future High Streets Fund project on Market Street is ongoing. The paper says the likelihood of delay to completion is high, and marketing and internal layout work is under way to maximise occupation.
findings.matters: A capital scheme delayed by building condition is a common cost and timing risk for regeneration projects, and other councils would want to compare how it is handled.
findings.figures: None stated.
findings.quote: Likelihood of delay to completion high due to the condition of the building being poorer than thought.

findings.headline: The council states it is highly likely not to be compliant in all areas of the forthcoming housing inspection
findings.detail: The risk note says an improvement plan is underway and that additional resources are being identified. The risk score for legislative compliance is unchanged at 12, with a target of 2.
findings.matters: A stated expectation of non-compliance ahead of an inspection is a compliance signal that a finance director or lender would want to track.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (current); target risk score 2.
findings.quote: it is highly likely that the council will not be compliant in all areas

findings.headline: The Regulator of Social Housing completed its inspection in July 2026, with the outcome still awaited
findings.detail: The paper says the outcome and the subsequent improvement plan are awaited. It says the improvement plan will replace the Social Housing Regulatory Programme and that this risk will then close. The risk note expects the regulatory inspection outcome at the end of October.
findings.matters: A regulatory intervention on housing would be a material governance event for a council and its lenders, and the paper shows its timing and the process that follows.

findings.quote: Regulator of Social Housing completed inspection in July 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1a Corporate Risk Register excluding risk 92026
findings.headline: The staff pay award is 3.3% against a budgeted 3%
findings.detail: The risk note records a staff pay award above budget, alongside other pressures including the cost of migrating IT systems to the cloud. It says some treasury management investment income may offset part of the pressure.
findings.matters: A pay award above budget is a common pressure on council budgets, and the paper shows the difference and the other cost pressures it sits alongside.

findings.headline: The three-year local government settlement for 2026/27 is described as more favourable than expected

findings.matters: Other councils planning against the same three-year settlement would want to see how a council reads a better-than-expected first year alongside a reducing grant in later years.

findings.quote: Despite a more favourable three year settlement for 2026/27 than had been expected

findings.detail: The risk note states that the current General Fund position needs balances and reserves to balance the budget. Work on the 2027/28 MTFS has started, with CMT and portfolio holders asked to find savings and additional income.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to know how far a council is drawing on reserves to balance its budget while savings remain unidentified.

findings.quote: the current GF budgetary position requires the use of balances and reserves to balance the budget

findings.headline: The committee's previous actions have progressed, but a consolidated action plan has not yet been developed.
findings.detail: The paper reports that several earlier actions have moved forward, but they are not tracked in one place. It recommends an action plan that records recommendations, owners, target dates and progress, with a target of April 2027.
findings.matters: A consolidated tracker of audit recommendations is how a finance director or external reader can confirm that control weaknesses identified by internal audit are being closed.
findings.figures: April 2027 target date
findings.quote: a consolidated action plan has not been developed.

findings.headline: Attendance records show 10 of 29 Members completed the council's finance training.

findings.matters: Member finance training completion is a measurable control that another council's finance team could compare against their own, and it shows how far the wider council's finance knowledge has been built.

findings.quote: attendance records show only 10 of 29 Members completed this.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Effectiveness
findings.headline: Members' average self-scored knowledge in the 2026 skills assessment was 1.8 out of 5 for counter fraud and treasury management and 2.0 out of 5 for organisational knowledge, governance and internal audit.
findings.detail: The paper reports the 2026 skills assessment results for the committee and proposes targeted training in the lower-scoring areas, with the Executive Director Finance and Commercial (S151 Officer) responsible by April 2027. Treasury management is one of the two lowest-scoring areas.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see how far the committee that oversees the council's audit and risk arrangements feels equipped to scrutinise treasury management, which bears on borrowing and investment decisions.
findings.figures: 1.8 out of 5 for counter fraud and treasury management; 2.0 out of 5 for organisational knowledge and governance; 2.0 out of 5 for internal audit; April 2027 target date
findings.quote: 1.8 for counter fraud and treasury management.

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update Qtr2 2026
findings.headline: Tamworth has set up a 'cost of living' working group in response to economic uncertainty from conflict in the Middle East.
findings.detail: The report identifies the conflict in the Middle East as an example of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty being monitored for possible escalation to the corporate risk register. It says action has been taken to stand up a cost of living working group to address the potential consequences.
findings.matters: A council creating a dedicated working group in response to a named external economic shock indicates how it expects that shock to affect residents and its own finances, which peer finance officers facing the same pressure would compare.
findings.quote: action was been taken to stand up a ‘cost of living’ working group to address the potential consequences

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update Qtr2 2026
findings.headline: Tamworth's CMT suggests the large Ankerside project may need escalation from departmental risk management to a Corporate Risk Project.
findings.detail: When comparing its corporate risks with similar-sized authorities, the report says most risks align, but further consideration may be needed for large projects, naming Ankerside. It asks whether departmental management is adequate or whether these risks should be escalated to the corporate register.
findings.matters: A large capital scheme whose risks may move up to corporate level is a signal about project governance and exposure, relevant to finance officers overseeing major schemes and to lenders assessing capital programme risk.
findings.quote: further consideration may need to be given to our large projects e.g. Ankerside, and whether it is adequate to manage these risks at operational/department level

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update Qtr2 2026
findings.headline: Risk 2, Governance and Legislative Compliance, has a higher current risk score at Quarter 2, with the justification documented in Appendix 1.
findings.detail: The report states that justification for the increase in the current risk score for Risk 2 is documented in Appendix 1 and shown as notes to the relevant risks. The high-risk profile for Quarter 1 remained at 50% after risk control measures, with the other 50% scored as Medium.
findings.matters: A rise in the score for a governance and legislative compliance risk at a council signals a change in the assessed exposure that a finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to understand, although the reasons sit in the appendix.
findings.figures: High-risk profile 50%; remaining risks 50% scored as Medium
findings.quote: Justification for the increase in current risk score for Risk 2 -Governance and Legislative Compliance has been documented in Appendix 1

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The paper states that Tamworth was to become part of the Southern and Mid Staffordshire unitary council on 1st April 2028, and that the timetable is now paused.
findings.detail: The paper says the pause on local government reorganisation brings further uncertainty, but the council must still set a balanced budget. A £500k reserve has been set aside for staffing costs of reorganisation, and reserves may be needed for aggregation and disaggregation costs.
findings.matters: A council whose future as a standalone authority is uncertain has to plan five years of budgets while the reorganisation timetable is unsettled, which affects lenders and peers alike.
findings.figures: £500k (reserve for reorganisation staffing costs); 1st April 2028 (original unitary date); 2031/32 (MTFS horizon)
findings.quote: Tamworth was to become part of Southern and Mid Staffordshire unitary council on 1st April 2028

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The 2026/27 local government pay award was agreed at 3.3%, above the 3% budgeted, with 3% assumed for 2027/28 and 2.5% thereafter.
findings.detail: The paper records the 2026/27 pay settlement at 3.3% against a 3% budget. The base budget assumes 3% for 2027/28 and 2.5% a year after, a point it lists among the uncertainties for the final budget.
findings.matters: A pay award above budget is a cost pressure that peers are also absorbing, and the assumed rates for later years are a sensitivity lenders would test.
findings.figures: 3.3% (2026/27 pay award); 3% (budgeted 2026/27); 3% (assumed 2027/28); 2.5% (assumed 2028/29 onwards)
findings.quote: Local Government pay for 2026/27 was agreed at 3.3%, in excess of the budgeted increase of 3%.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The HRA Capital Financing Requirement stands at £75.312m, with £2.585m of planned borrowing in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper notes that borrowing for unsupported costs will mean higher debt interest costs for the HRA. The GF CFR is separately reported at £6.007m.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing HRA debt levels with peers will want the CFR, planned borrowing, and the interest cost of unsupported borrowing together.
findings.figures: £75.312m (HRA CFR); £2.585m (planned 2026/27 HRA borrowing); £6.007m (GF CFR)
findings.quote: The current HRA Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) stands at £75.312m with planned borrowing in 2026/27 of £2.585m.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The HRA capital programme has a funding gap of £6.793m over five years, against a five-year programme of £47,171,500.
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA gap is based on current indications and is subject to review after an updated stock condition survey. It notes that energy efficiency measures cannot currently be funded, and the financing table shows £6,793,300 of unsupported borrowing across the five years.
findings.matters: A landlord HRA with an unfunded five-year capital gap and rising unsupported borrowing is a key test of its long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £6.793m (5-year HRA funding gap); £47,171,500 (5-year HRA capital programme); £6,793,300 (HRA unsupported borrowing)
findings.quote: current indications suggest that there will be a significant funding gap for the HRA capital programme - £6.793m over 5 years

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The General Fund capital programme would leave a £0.797m shortfall over five years, to be funded from revenue, if the programme progresses unchanged.
findings.detail: The paper says the GF capital forecast cannot fund all submitted schemes, and any shortfall would need revenue funding that worsens the revenue position. It asks members to consider where spend can be reduced. The GF CFR stands at £6.007m, with £25k of planned 2026/27 borrowing.
findings.matters: A capital shortfall that moves to revenue is a direct link between capital ambition and reserves, which lenders and peers examine together.
findings.figures: £0.797m (5-year GF capital shortfall); £467k (3-year shortfall); £0.5million (minimum GF capital balance); £6.007m (GF CFR); £25k (planned 2026/27 borrowing)
findings.quote: this would mean a £0.797m shortfall over the next 5 years (£467k over 3 years) which would have to be funded from revenue

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: A swimming subsidy is proposed for a further two years at £127k in 2027/28, reversing part of a 2025/26 saving.
findings.detail: The schedule shows the swimming subsidy extension at £127.00k in 2027/28 and removed in 2029/30. The paper records that a 2025/26 decision removed the swimming subsidy, with a £118,000 budget saving.
findings.matters: A reversal of a prior-year saving on a leisure subsidy is an example of a service decision that a peer finance officer would want to track against the original saving.
findings.figures: 127.00 £000 (2027/28 extension); (118,000) (2025/26 removal of swimming subsidy)
findings.quote: Extension of swimming subidy for a further two years

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: Actions completed under the Financial Resilience Plan include the service review of Outdoor Events and the Assembly Rooms.
findings.detail: The paper says the plan responds to the 2024 LGA Corporate Peer Challenge, which recommended a costed and deliverable savings plan. It states that other workstreams, including underspend identification, zero-based budgeting and a review of reserves, are continuing.
findings.matters: Peers working through the same LGA recommendations can compare which workstreams have produced completed reviews and which are still in progress.
findings.quote: Actions have already been completed in a number of areas, including the service review of Outdoor Events and the Assembly Rooms

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: Increased car parking income of up to £256k a year is listed as a proposal with options still to be considered.
findings.detail: The savings schedule includes a car parking income increase, with the paper saying options are still to be considered. Other planning-related income items are also included, including a national default planning fee schedule from December 2026.
findings.matters: A savings line that is still at the options stage is one a peer or lender would expect to see evidenced before it is counted against the budget gap.
findings.figures: up to £256k pa (car parking income, (256.19) £000 in schedule); (68.00) £000 (planning fee income, 27/28)
findings.quote: Increased car parking income - options to be considered up to £256k pa

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The paper states that income from Ankerside shopping centre tenants is uncertain, while running and maintenance costs continue.
findings.detail: The paper identifies Ankerside as a specific risk to the budget, because tenant income is uncertain while significant expenditure is still needed. The budget proposes replacing current management arrangements with a directly employed Head of Service for commercial lettings, shown as a £60k saving.
findings.matters: A council carrying a shopping centre with uncertain tenant income is a standard exposure for lenders and for finance directors comparing commercial property risk.
findings.figures: (60.00) £000 (proposed Head of Service saving, 27/28)
findings.quote: there are risks with regard to the Ankerside shopping centre whereby income streams from tenants are uncertain

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The government's ambition is for councils to retain 70% of business rates by the end of the decade, with the effect on funding not yet quantified.
findings.detail: The paper reports the Chancellor's 28 October 2026 budget ambition under the devolution agenda. It states that the resulting changes to local authority funding are not yet quantified and will be detailed in the settlement process.
findings.matters: A move to 70% retention would change the basis of every district's funding and is a material uncertainty for medium-term plans.
findings.figures: 70% (target business rates retention by end of decade)
findings.quote: with the aim that local authorities will be able to retain 70% of business rates revenues by the end of the decade

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility payment is notified at £1.203m for 2026/27, up from £1.071m received in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper treats the EPR payment as ongoing for MTFS purposes, though it says prudent assumptions have been made about future years. The payment sits outside Core Spending Power and is expected to offset additional waste collection costs.
findings.matters: EPR is a new and outside-the-settlement income stream for waste collection, and its treatment as ongoing is a judgement a finance director would test.
findings.quote: Tamworth received £1.071m in 2025/26 and our anticipated EPR payment for the financial year 2026/27 has been notified as £1.203m.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The paper says the 2026/27 settlement was favourable to Tamworth against earlier projections, which had expected all retained business rates growth to be lost.
findings.detail: The paper records that the government changed its pooling-gains methodology after the provisional settlement, which made a significant difference to the RSG Tamworth expected. An 'Adjustment Support Grant' of £594,880 was added for 2026/27 to compensate.
findings.matters: A tariff authority that expected to lose its business rates growth and has instead gained time to adjust is a useful reference for peers facing the same reset.
findings.figures: £594,880 (Adjustment Support Grant, 2026/27)
findings.quote: The settlement was favourable to Tamworth, compared to previous projections

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant falls from £3,783,682 in 2026/27 to £3,433,775 in 2027/28 and £3,060,260 in 2028/29 under the phased settlement.
findings.detail: The paper says the new funding model is phased in over the three-year settlement, which reduces RSG each year before the grant rises by 2% a year from 2029/30. Several grants, including New Homes Bonus and the Temporary Accommodation element of Homelessness Prevention Grant, were rolled into RSG for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A fall in RSG of this size at a district council changes the balance between government grant and locally raised income, which lenders and peers track closely.
findings.quote: The new funding model is being phased in over the three year settlement period, and this is reflected in the reducing amounts of RSG.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The paper models council tax at 2.99%, £5.00 and 0% a year, and the 0% option shows a £6.103m shortfall over five years.
findings.detail: The 2.99% option is the MTFS assumption, at a Band D of £221.43 in 2027/28. The paper says capping for district councils is expected at the higher of £5 or 3.0%, and the 0% option leaves the council with a shortfall of £2.197m over four years.
findings.matters: Council tax policy and capping thresholds determine whether a district council can close its gap without reserves, a question every peer modelling the same pressures will face.
findings.figures: 2.99% (£6.43) 2027/28 increase; £221.43 (Band D 2027/28 at 2.99%); £2.197m shortfall over 4 years and £6.103m over 5 years (0% option); higher of £5 or 3.0% (capping threshold)
findings.quote: with a shortfall of £2.197m over 4 years and £6.103m over the 5 year period

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: Social rent increase for 2027/28 is set at 4.5%, the maximum under the Rent Standard, with each 1% worth c.£244k a year.
findings.detail: The paper applies CPI of 3.5% (September 2026) plus 1% to give 4.5% for 2027/28, with 3% a year assumed after. It also notes that rent convergence, if adopted, would allow unconverged rents to rise by CPI plus 1% plus £1 in 2027/28 and plus £2 from 2028/29. The modelled no-increase option would reduce rent income by £13,277,070 over five years against the CPI-plus-1% option.
findings.matters: Rent policy is a direct lever on HRA income and so on the capital funding gap, and the convergence option is a new policy decision for the sector.
findings.figures: 4.5% (2027/28 increase); c.£244k p.a. per 1% (£3.920m cumulative over 5 years); £13,277,070 (no-increase option, reduced rent over 5 years)
findings.quote: the budgeted increase for 2027/28 will be 4.5% in line with the maximum allowed by the Rent Standard

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: HRA balances are £3.505m in 2027/28, against £3.925m in the approved MTFS, and rise to £6.735m in 2029/30 against £5.217m previously forecast.
findings.detail: The HRA forecast is lower than the approved MTFS for 2027/28 but higher by 2029/30, reaching £12.425m by 2031/32. The paper says the forecast includes £599k of pressures over five years but excludes the HRA capital business plan update and additional repairs and Regulator of Social Housing costs.
findings.matters: The HRA balance path depends on rent policy and capital funding, and the exclusions mean the paper itself flags the figures as incomplete.
findings.quote: HRA balances of £3.505m by 2027/28 (compared to £3.925m as part of the approved MTFS forecast in February 2026)

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: A 2025/26 overspend reduces the 2027/28 General Fund balance brought forward by £936k, subject to final accounts audit.
findings.detail: The paper records a £936k reduction in balances brought forward from 2025/26 because of an overspend, shown for 2027/28 only and subject to confirmation through the final accounts audit. A separate £78k projected outturn pressure is shown for Q2 2026/27.
findings.matters: A finance director can test whether the overspend will be confirmed at audit and whether the Q2 2026/27 projection is recovered by year end.
findings.figures: £936k (reduction in balances b/f, 27/28 only); £78k (projected outturn Q2 2026/27, 26/27 only)
findings.quote: Reduced balances b/f from 2025/26 due to overspend (subject to confirmation of final accounts audit)

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: The paper states that the MTFS 'continues to require the use of reserves and balances to balance the budget'.
findings.detail: The executive summary says the 2026/27 budget was balanced with reserves and balances, despite a more favourable settlement than expected. The paper describes this reliance as not sustainable over the medium to long term.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance the revenue budget is the core sustainability test a lender or external auditor applies to a council in this position.
findings.quote: the MTFS continues to require the use of reserves and balances to balance the budget, which is not sustainable over the medium to long term.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2027/28
findings.headline: General Fund balances are projected at £6.252m in 2027/28, rising to £2.091m in 2029/30, with a £3.650m shortfall by 2031/32 including the £500k minimum balance.
findings.detail: The base budget update lowers 2027/28 General Fund balances from £6.270m to £6.252m and raises 2029/30 balances from £357k to £2.091m. The paper's forecast then shows a £3.650m shortfall by 2031/32, measured after the £500k minimum balance.
findings.matters: A finance director at Tamworth or a peer council can compare the year in which balances turn negative with their own reserve runway and minimum-balance policy.

findings.quote: with a shortfall of £3.650m by 2031/32 (including the minimum level of balances of £500k)

findings.detail: The paper links treasury operations and cash flow planning to the Financial Resilience Plan and to local government reorganisation. It says there are no direct reorganisation implications in the recommendations.
findings.matters: Councils in reorganisation areas are being asked to show how their treasury and cash planning will carry into any new unitary body, which is relevant to other councils facing the same change.

findings.quote: ensuring that it enters any new unitary arrangements from the strongest possible financial position

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report

findings.matters: A council that lends to other councils is also a counterparty to them, so the rates and terms it accepts show what peer councils are paying for short-term cash.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Tamworth's property fund valuation was £6.699m at 30 September 2026, an overall loss of £1.207m since the 2022 gain
findings.detail: The paper says the funds recovered after 2020 and gained £1.132m by March 2022 before falling again. The paper also reports £86,537 in dividends from the funds to 30 September 2026, which it says is part of the 2026/27 revenue budget; the text separately gives £276k for 2026/27 and £442k for 2025/26. The paper says the Hermes fund is no longer held.
findings.matters: Property fund losses reduce the capital value of a council's treasury holdings and the dividends that support its revenue budget, which is a risk other councils holding similar funds will want to measure.

findings.matters: Rising opportunities to restructure debt, with none yet taken, is a position a lender or peer finance team would want to track as rates move.

findings.detail: The paper calls the internal borrowing approach prudent and cost effective in the current climate, but says it will need monitoring if gilt yields stay high at the long end of the curve.
findings.matters: A council choosing to use its own cash rather than new borrowing while gilt yields are elevated is a decision other finance directors may be weighing for themselves.

findings.detail: The paper attributes the forecast to increased cash balances from capital re-profiling and to interest rates higher than expected. The budget and forecast are stated as at September Period 6.

findings.headline: Market interest rate expectations have reversed; council's under-borrowed strategy faces rising rate risk
findings.detail: The council adopted an under-borrowed position for 2025/26, using cash reserves rather than borrowing because investment returns were expected to exceed borrowing costs. As of early April 2026, the market expects Bank Rate to rise from 3.75% to 4-4.25%, contrary to forecasts of reductions made when the strategy was set. The Middle East conflict is expected to push inflation above 4.5%, potentially requiring higher rates. This reversal threatens the fundamental assumption underpinning the under-borrowed strategy.
findings.matters: If the council is forced to borrow at elevated PWLB rates (now 5.28%-6.29% depending on term), the under-borrowed position becomes expensive; the strategy was not hedged against rate rises.

findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: No new borrowing undertaken, with council citing elevated long-term rates as constraint
findings.detail: The council undertook no external borrowing in 2025/26 despite a Capital Financing Requirement of £74m and external debt of £63m. The reason given is the elevated cost of long-term borrowing (PWLB rates peaked above 5%), which the council judged unaffordable.
findings.matters: The decision not to borrow despite capital needs signals that the council views borrowing as unaffordable at current rates and is instead consuming reserves—a short-term strategy that cannot continue indefinitely as reserves deplete.

findings.matters: Lower revenue reserves reduce financial resilience and the council's ability to absorb unexpected cost pressures, changes in income, or delays in savings delivery.

findings.detail: The council's usable capital receipts, which originate from the sale of the Golf Course and provide flexible capital finance without borrowing, have fallen dramatically from £10.582m to £3.472m. findings.matters: Capital receipts are the most flexible source of capital finance; their depletion means future capital investment becomes dependent on borrowing at rates the council currently views as unaffordable.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Refuse joint arrangement cost increased by £581k, partially offset by reduced recycling credits.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: CPI inflation forecast in MTFS (2.8%) is now expected to reach 4%, adding to budget pressure.
findings.detail: The medium-term financial strategy was built on a CPI inflation forecast of 2.8%. The outturn report now indicates that CPI could rise to 4% by year end, significantly higher than assumed. This will feed through to contract inflation, energy costs, and demand-driven services across the budget, and comes at a time when the council is already running a structural deficit.
findings.matters: In a tight budget environment with little room for variance, CPI tracking 40% above forecast means the council has a shortfall it cannot absorb. The cost-of-living crisis is explicitly noted as impacting collection performance on council tax and rents.
findings.figures: MTFS assumed 2.8% CPI; indications that CPI could reach 4% by year end.
findings.quote: A CPI inflation rate of 2.8% was assumed in the MTFS forecasts, however, indications are that this could be significantly higher, possibly up to 4% by the year end.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Pay award will escalate beyond budget: employers offered 3.3% but MTFS assumed 3%.
findings.detail: The MTFS was built on a 3% pay award assumption. Local government employers have offered 3.3%, which the report says is certain to incur additional costs. This applies both to the base pay uplift and cascading increases in employers' NI and superannuation. The trades unions have rejected the offer for non-chief officers, suggesting further pressure is likely.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 50–60% of local authority revenue costs. A 0.3% underestimation on a large base, plus NI and pension uplift, can rapidly exceed budget. The council's narrow revenue margins make this material.
findings.figures: Assumed 3% pay award in MTFS; employers offered 3.3% (accepted for chief officers, rejected by unions for other staff). Includes additional employers' NI and superannuation cost on top.
findings.quote: The MTFS included provision for a pay award of 3% for staff in 2026/27, however, local government employers have offered 3.3%, which, whilst accepted for chief officers, has been rejected by the trades unions at this stage for other staff. It is therefore certain that additional salaries costs will be incurred, including an increased employers' NI and superannuation cost on top of this.

These costs have not yet been quantified and sit outside the current MTFS, adding to future budget pressure at a time when the council is already structurally in deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on all material future costs. Unquantified LGR costs during a period of structural deficits represent a double pincer: the council is already running out of reserves while facing unknown additional calls on those reserves.

findings.quote: Additional resources including staffing, potential consultancy support and legal advice will be required to progress with local government reorganisation and community governance review projects over the next two years, which are yet to be quantified.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Universal credit tenants in arrears at 42.3% of council tenants, creating a rent collection risk.

The overall rent arrears increased by £9k year-on-year to £467k (excluding former tenants), and total arrears including former tenant arrears reached £2.316m, up £113k. The council recorded only three evictions since April 2025, suggesting enforcement is not keeping pace with arrears growth.
findings.matters: Rent is a key council revenue source, and a lender is exposed to collection risk if the council's largest tenant population is increasingly unable to pay. UC tenants are systemically vulnerable to income shocks.
findings.figures: 42.3% of council tenants on UC in arrears (prior year 40.4%). Rent arrears (excl. former tenants) £467k, up £9k. Total arrears £2.316m, up £113k. UC claimants in Tamworth increased to 11,591 (from 10,815 prior year).
findings.quote: Currently, 42.3% of universal credit claimants who are council tenants are behind with their rent (40.4% at the end of March 2025).

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Budgets are currently being balanced by the use of reserves and balances which is not sustainable.

The report explicitly warns that reserves are being used unsustainably to bridge a structural gap, and savings of approaching £3.5m per year will be required from 2029/30 onwards to balance budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can service debt from operations or is in a managed decline mode. Unsustainable reserve-draining means the council is consuming its financial buffer rather than living within its means.
findings.figures: General Fund balances £9.804m at year-end (increased by £1.050m from budget). Savings approaching £3.5m per year required from 2029/30. Three-year settlement to 2028/29, after which deficits accelerate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position, betting on falling interest rates, with no new borrowing planned across 2026/27-2028/29 despite rising capital financing requirement.
findings.detail: The council has a capital financing requirement (CFR) of £81.319m in 2026/27 but only £63.060m in external debt. The under-borrowing position reaches £18.259m in 2026/27 and grows to £21.821m by 2028/29. The strategy relies on current forecasts that interest rates will fall. The treasury advisor notes that 'Bank Rate remains relatively elevated in 2026 even if some rate cuts arise' but the council is still postponing borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the risk of this strategy if interest rate forecasts prove wrong. If rates do not fall as expected, the council may face higher borrowing costs later. The strategy also depends on continuing to have sufficient cash reserves to cover the CFR without borrowing.
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels, albeit only once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by restrictive near-term monetary policy. That is, Bank Rate remains relatively elevated in 2026 even if some rate cuts arise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Growing Housing Revenue Account debt burden, with debt per dwelling projected to reach £20,172 by 2028/29, up from £17,501 in 2024/25.
findings.detail: HRA debt is increasing steadily across the planning period. The ratio of HRA debt to revenues is 300% in 2024/25, rising to 306% in 2026/27 and holding at 306% by 2028/29. Debt per dwelling rises from £17,501 to £20,172 over the four-year period. The council's HRA is increasingly leveraged.
findings.matters: Lenders use HRA debt ratios to assess housing finance sustainability. A 306% ratio and growing per-dwelling debt suggests increasing pressure on tenant rents and reduced financial flexibility for the housing service.
findings.quote: HRA Debt to Revenues Ratio Actual 300% [2024/25], Estimate 306% [2026/27]. HRA Debt per Dwelling £'000 2024/25 17.501, 2028/29 20.172

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Council reserves declining by £20.6m over four years, from £43.8m to £23.1m, as the council uses reserves to fund capital projects.
findings.detail: The council's Fund Balances and Reserves are projected to fall significantly: from £43.774m in 2024/25 to £28.492m in 2026/27, reaching £23.119m by 2028/29. This decline reflects the council's strategy of using internal reserves to finance capital expenditure rather than borrowing externally. Total core funds available for investment fall from £58.736m to £25.288m.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about deteriorating financial resilience. Falling reserves reduce the council's buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and constrain future borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: Year End Resources 2024/25 Actual £43.774m, 2026/27 Estimate £28.492m, 2028/29 Estimate £23.119m. Expected Investments 65.154m [2024/25] to 16.523m [2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation into unitary structure from April 2028 creates execution risk on savings plan
findings.detail: The council is likely to merge into a larger unitary authority from 1st April 2028 — a restructuring that will require significant management time and resources to implement. The council has established a Project Management Office for reorganisation planning. This 18-month window (from April 2026) coincides exactly with the period when the council needs to identify and deliver £1m+ annual savings to rebalance the budget.
findings.matters: Reorganisation diverts senior management attention from operational efficiency at precisely the time the council needs to execute a major savings programme. The dual agenda creates execution risk: either reorganisation slips and delays necessary action, or the savings agenda suffers.
findings.figures: Unitary merger effective 1st April 2028; PMO established for reorganisation; £1m savings required from 2027/28
findings.quote: Pending local government reorganisation will also bring challenges and involve significant additional resources to implement. The need for a Project Management Office has been reflected in the budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Government changed business rates funding methodology mid-MTFS process, creating planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's MTFS was drafted on the basis of the Government's provisional settlement published in December 2025. On 9th February 2026 — after Cabinet and scrutiny review — the Government announced significant changes to the methodology for distributing retained business rates through pooling, with material impact to Tamworth. This late change came after the budget had been through formal scrutiny.
findings.matters: Late policy changes create budget risk. The MTFS may need revision. Tamworth's funding position depends on Government decisions over which it has no control, and precedent shows these can shift with little notice.
findings.figures: Provisional settlement December 2025; final settlement announcement with methodology changes 9th February 2026
findings.quote: This contained some significant changes to the figures published in the provisional settlement in December, which had formed the basis for reports to Cabinet and Joint Scrutiny (Budgets) in January. This included a change in the methodology for distributing retained business rates

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund reserves will be drawn down by £1.1m in 2026/27, beginning pattern of depletion across MTFS
findings.detail: The council is applying £1,096,790 from General Fund reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget. Across the forecast period to 2028/29, reserves continue to be drawn down each year. While the council will maintain minimum balances of £500k through to 2028/29, the underlying position is that current revenue and expenditure cannot be balanced without reserve support.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve drawdowns indicate the council is living beyond its means on a recurring basis. This erodes financial flexibility and reduces capacity to respond to unexpected demands or income shocks.
findings.figures: £1,096,790 transfer from General Fund Revenue Balances in 2026/27; reserve drawdowns continuing across 2027/28, 2028/29 to cover ongoing deficits
findings.quote: the sum of £1,096,790 be transferred from General Fund Revenue Balances in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund has structural deficit requiring £1m annual savings from 2027/28 to avoid reserve depletion
findings.detail: The council faces deficits in every year of the forecast period. Reserve drawdowns can cover these in the short term but are unsustainable beyond 2028/29. The MTFS explicitly states that to balance the budget from 2027/28 onwards, the council must identify and deliver £1m+ in annual savings. These savings have not yet been identified.
findings.matters: Unidentified, undelivered savings are red flags for lenders. A £1m annual saving from a General Fund budget of £12.6m is material. Whether the council can find and deliver this by 2027/28 — while managing reorganisation — will determine financial stability.
findings.figures: Net Cost of Services £12,573k in 2026/27; General Fund deficit of £1,096k covered by reserve transfer; savings of at least £1m per year required from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Whilst this can be met from General Fund reserves over the short term, savings of at least £1m per year are required from 2027/28 in order to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 TMSS
findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy explicitly depends on cash reserves; no contingency if rates don't fall as forecast
findings.detail: The Council states it is 'using cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow as a temporary measure' instead of borrowing. The strategy acknowledges this is prudent only 'as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall'. However, if this forecast proves wrong and the Council has depleted reserves (falling to £23m by 2028/29), it will be forced to borrow at higher-than-forecast rates with minimal financial buffer.
findings.matters: The Council's financial stability over the forecast period is contingent on a specific interest rate outcome. Failure of that outcome leaves no fallback position.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement vs External Debt creates £18.259m gap in 2026/27 funded from reserves. Expected investments £25.596m by 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt, as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 TMSS

findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt rising from £70.507m (2025/26) to £75.312m (2026/27), driven by significant HRA capital expenditure of £12.163m. The debt-to-revenue ratio is 306% in 2026/27 (HRA revenues only £24.615m), up from 300% in 2024/25. This is a high leverage position for a single service area, particularly given the constraints on HRA rent-setting.
findings.matters: High HRA debt ratios reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to rental income shocks or capital cost overruns.
findings.figures: HRA Debt 2025/26: £70.507m, 2026/27: £75.312m, 2028/29: £79.518m. HRA Debt to Revenues Ratio 2026/27: 306%. HRA capital expenditure 2026/27: £12.163m.

This reflects the Council's strategy of using internal cash reserves rather than borrowing to fund a £81.3m Capital Financing Requirement. Once reserves approach critical levels, the Council will be forced to borrow regardless of interest rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when a council will have no choice but to access debt markets at potentially unfavourable rates, and how thin the buffer for unexpected demand becomes.

findings.detail: Due to the 2026 revaluation introducing uneven property value shifts across sectors and regions, councils remain uncertain how these changes affect their income. Final estimates are not confirmed until late January—after the budget has been formally approved.
findings.matters: The council is setting its 2026/27 budget without final confirmation of income from a source representing £16.9m of retained cash. Material variance after approval creates mid-year budget pressure.

findings.headline: Appeals risk from 2026 revaluation rated High; expected to increase substantially from economic downturn and pandemic effects
findings.detail: Appeals against new rateable values are categorized as High risk in the council's risk register. The paper states the risk of appeals increases substantially due to current economic climate and Covid aftermath, directly reducing the council's Business Rates income.
findings.matters: Appeals refunds are hard to predict and reduce cash received. High risk means actual income could materially underperform the £42.2m estimated yield.

findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's budget balance needs to understand that a major funding source has contracted below planning assumptions, creating a hole that must be filled from reserves or cuts.

findings.detail: The Business Rates Reset effective April 2026 realigns the baseline and redistributes growth gains accumulated since 2013. The paper explicitly warns that councils which have grown their local business rate base will lose the additional income generated by that growth, directly affecting Tamworth's retained share.
findings.matters: Business Rates is a significant part of the council's core funding (estimated retained £16.9m). This policy redistributes money away from growing councils to others, reducing predictable income.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund portfolio down £1.581m cumulatively since 2021
findings.detail: Property fund valuations have fallen from £10.143m (31 March 2025) to £6.892m (30 September 2025). Cumulative loss since March 2021 is £1.581m. The council was forcibly exited from the Federated Hermes fund when the merged vehicle restricted eligibility to UK pensions, realizing £3.528m from a £4.056m original investment.
findings.matters: Real erosion of financial reserves through underperforming property investments. Forced exit due to fund restructuring demonstrates exposure to investment risks outside the council's control. Cumulative £1.6m loss material to overall reserve position.
findings.figures: Valuation fell from £10.143m (31/03/2025) to £6.892m (30/09/2025); cumulative loss since 2021 of £1.581m; Federated Hermes returned £3.528m on £4.056m original investment

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme slipping by £5.182m (12.8%) to 2026/27
findings.detail: Of the £40.567m capital budget for 2025/26, only £35.385m is predicted to be spent in-year. The £5.182m slippage defers capital works to 2026/27. Associated borrowing need is also deferred: £1.830m required in 2025/26 against the £4.430m originally budgeted. No explanation is given for the underspend.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage signals potential delivery issues—either resource constraints, procurement delays, or overly optimistic planning. Deferred infrastructure spending pushes borrowing and its associated costs into the next year, affecting the council's medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: Capital budget £40.567m; predicted outturn £35.385m; slippage £5.182m (12.8% of budget); borrowing need deferred from £4.430m to £1.830m

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds
findings.headline: £1.12m reserve established to protect against property fund value declines
findings.detail: The council has set aside £1.12m specifically to hedge against shortfalls in property fund value, which would otherwise require a charge to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. This suggests concern about the valuation of the council's property investments.
findings.matters: Significant exposure to property valuations is material for lenders; if property values fall sharply, the council may have to revalue assets downward and exhaust reserves, or face accounting charges that worsen the financial position.
findings.figures: £1.12m reserve balance; required 'to mitigate effect of any shortfall/reduction in property fund value'

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds

The council explicitly notes the fund is 'Likely to be required to balance 26/27 MTFS', indicating non-recurring revenue sources are being used for recurring costs.
findings.matters: Reliance on volatile reserves to balance recurring budgets indicates structural budget pressure; this approach is unsustainable if reserves are depleted or if business rates fall further.

findings.quote: £500k released in 24/25 to support balanced budget and a further £500k contribution will be used in 25/26. Likely to be required to balance 26/27 MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds
findings.headline: Ankerside shopping centre consumed £3.97m from reserves in one year despite receiving £1.98m additional funding

The council retained £170k for 'potential revenue losses/capital investment required', signalling the centre is not generating expected revenue and requires ongoing subsidy.
findings.matters: A major asset requiring sustained capital/revenue subsidy is a risk to the council's financial sustainability; a lender would need to understand whether the shopping centre will ever be self-supporting or if this is an indefinite drain on cash.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26

findings.detail: PWLB certainty rates have risen materially: 10-year rates moved from 4.70% (1 April) to 5.53% (30 September); 25-year from 5.95% to 6.23%; 50-year from 5.63% to 5.98%. The council is deferring new borrowing by using £12.953m of cash reserves, a prudent tactic that depends on continued low gilt yields. The paper explicitly flags that this strategy requires ongoing monitoring if yields remain elevated, particularly at the longer end of the curve where volatility has been highest.
findings.matters: Sustained elevated gilt yields increase future borrowing costs; the council's current strategy of using cash reserves to avoid new debt is only viable if yields fall as forecast; if they do not, the council will face higher debt servicing costs
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rates 4.70%–5.53% over period; 25-year 5.95%–6.23%; 50-year 5.63%–5.98%; current internal borrowing £12.953m
findings.quote: This is a prudent and cost effective approach in the current economic climate but will require ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated, particularly at the longer-end of the yield curve (25 to 50 years).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund valuations have fallen £1.581m since March 2025, with forced liquidation of Federated Hermes fund at a loss
findings.detail: Tamworth's property fund investments total £6.892m as at 30 September 2025, down from £10.411m at 31 March 2025.
